rationale: Scoring happens within each cohort, but the four sites differ in pre-analytics and MS runs, which shifts each protein's level by site. Centring every log2 protein on its own site's median (an unsupervised step that uses only `meta['site']`, not labels) removes those shifts. The L2 logistic model can then learn the AD-vs-non-AD differences inside each site, which is exactly what the metric rewards.

I'm adding a second, knowledge-driven model and averaging its ranks with the existing whole-proteome L2 logistic regression. The second model is a logistic regression restricted to a small panel of proteins that Bader et al. 2020 and later CSF AD proteomics reported. The panel covers the glycolysis and 14-3-3 proteins that go up (SMOC1, YWHAG, PKM, ALDOA, MDH1, GDA), glial and inflammation markers (CHI3L1, SPP1, GFAP, TREM2), neuronal damage markers (NEFL, MAPT, NRGN, UCHL1) and synaptic proteins that go down (NPTX2, VGF, SCG2, CHGA). With n≈137, roughly 1,000 noisy features can drown this concentrated biology. A low-dimensional prior-driven model should give more stable rankings within each site, and averaging it with the data-driven model hedges against panel proteins that are missing or noisy here. I haven't run this yet; the harness score will show whether it helps.

I'm adding a third member to the rank-average ensemble: a compound-covariate (diagonal-LDA-style) score on the prior-biology panel. Each panel protein, standardized on the training fold, is weighted by its training-fold Welch t-statistic, and the weighted values are summed. With n≈137 and correlated panel proteins (the glycolysis/14-3-3 module goes up, the synaptic/neurosecretory module goes down), this estimator ignores covariance. That makes it more stable than a multivariate logistic fit, which can give correlated proteins unstable, opposite-signed weights. So it should give more robust rankings within each site. Not run yet, so I don't know if it beats the current 0.874; the harness score will tell.

The 70% quantification filter likely removes the low-abundance, brain-derived panel proteins that matter most for the panel model (MAPT, NRGN, NEFL, GFAP, CHIT1, some neurosecretory peptides). Their DIA missingness depends on abundance, so a missing value probably means "low level". The panel model will now keep any panel protein quantified in at least 30% of training samples and fill gaps with the half-minimum value, so missingness can count as signal. The whole-proteome model stays at the strict 70% filter.

CSF samples carry varying amounts of blood (erythrocyte) contamination, and many glycolytic and housekeeping proteins in the panel (GAPDH, ENO1, LDHA/B, PGK1, TPI1, PPIA, PEBP1, SOD1, PARK7, CALM) are very abundant in red cells. That can confound the AD glycolysis signal and add noise to the whole-proteome model. Inside `featurize`, which never sees labels, I compute a per-sample erythrocyte contamination score from red-cell-specific proteins (HBA1/HBB/HBD/CA1/PRDX2/CAT/BLVRB/SLC4A1/ALAS2, following Bader 2020's quality-marker idea). I then regress that score out of every non-marker protein, using only the samples where the protein was quantified, before the unchanged ensemble runs.

I'm adding a third member to the rank-average ensemble: a low-dimensional logistic regression on five prior-biology module scores (glycolysis/14-3-3, glial/inflammation, neuronal injury, synaptic/neurosecretory, amyloid/lipid/complement). Each module score is the mean of its proteins after standardizing on the training fold. Averaging the correlated proteins within a module should cancel per-protein DIA noise and imputation error, and with only 5 weights to fit, the rankings within each site should be more stable at n≈137.

I'm adding a second label-free nuisance correction in `featurize`, built the same way as the erythrocyte step that was kept in round 5. A per-sample blood–CSF-barrier leakage score (the mean z-score of liver/plasma-derived proteins such as ALB, IGs, fibrinogen, HP and APOA/B) is regressed out of every other protein. Barrier leakiness varies a lot between people and, after median normalisation, artificially lowers or raises the brain-derived AD proteins, so removing it should leave cleaner AD contrasts within each site. Not run yet; the harness score will show whether it helps.

Some modules mix proteins that move in opposite directions in AD. For example, the amyloid/complement module has APP and SPARCL1 next to APOE, CLU and C3, and neuronal-injury markers sit next to synaptic BASP1/STMN1. A plain mean of z-scores lets those members cancel each other out. This change gives each module member the sign of its loading on the module's first principal component, fitted on the training fold without labels, so the module score adds up co-varying signal instead of averaging it away.

I'm adding a fourth member to the rank average: an L2 logistic regression on about 30 co-expression module scores. The modules are learned from the training fold's whole proteome (proteins quantified in ≥70% of samples), without labels, by Ward clustering of the standardized protein profiles. CSF proteome variation comes in correlated blocks (cell type, secretory pathway, barrier). Averaging within data-driven modules should cut per-protein noise, as the five prior-biology modules did. It should also pick up AD-related co-expression programs that the hand-written panel misses, with only about 30 weights to fit at n≈137. I haven't run this yet; the harness score will show whether it helps.

I'm adding a fourth member to the rank average, a fixed-weight log-ratio score: the mean z-score of glycolysis/14-3-3 proteins that rise in AD (YWHAG, SMOC1, PKM, ALDOA) minus the mean z-score of neuronal pentraxin and VGF synaptic proteins that fall in AD (NPTX2, NPTXR, NPTX1, VGF). This follows the YWHAG:NPTX2 ratio reported as a strong CSF AD and cognitive-decline marker. The score fits no weights, only its overall sign is checked on the training fold, and taking a ratio cancels shared per-sample dilution and CSF-production effects. So it should give within-site rankings that stay stable at n≈137, which the fitted members can't promise.

The fixed-weight YWHAG:NPTX2 ratio was the biggest single gain so far (+0.026), which suggests weight-free, prior-biology scores give the most stable within-site rankings at n≈137. I'm adding a second weight-free score as a fifth rank-average member: a tau-surrogate sum. It is the mean training-standardized z-score of the proteins that rise in AD CSF and track CSF tau (Bader 2020 / Johnson 2022): MAPT and NRGN for neuronal injury, SMOC1, TMSB10, MDH1 and GDA (the top tau-correlated proteins in the Bader set), and CHI3L1 and SPP1 for glial response. As with the ratio, the only thing fitted is its overall sign on the training fold. It mostly uses proteins the current ratio leaves out, so it should add a separate low-variance view.

The score is within-site AUROC, but each member's scores are currently ranked across all test samples pooled together. If a member's scores shift by cohort (site effects on the whole-proteome or panel fits), that cohort's samples bunch into a narrow pooled-rank band, which quietly lowers that member's weight inside the cohort. Ranking each member within the site of each test sample (`meta_test['site']` is used only to harmonize score scales, not as a predictor) gives every member equal weight inside every cohort. That matches the metric directly, and no labels are involved.

The weight-free YWHAG:NPTX2-style ratio gave the biggest single gain (+0.026). Adding a second weight-free member (round 11) lowered the score, which suggests the ratio's stable signal is being diluted by the three fitted members, which are noisy at n≈110 per training fold. So I'm giving the ratio double weight in the within-site rank average, making the fixed prior-biology contrast count as much as two fitted models, while leaving every member unchanged. This hasn't been run yet; the harness score will show whether it helps.

The YWHAG:NPTX2-style member now subtracts the mean z-score of the down proteins from the mean z-score of the up proteins. Dividing each protein by its own SD gives the proteins unequal effective weights in log space. So shared per-sample multiplicative factors (CSF dilution, total-protein and production rate) no longer cancel, and low-variance proteins have their noise amplified. I am replacing it with a true equal-weight log2 ratio, mean log2(up) minus mean log2(down), which is how the literature YWHAG:NPTX2 ratio is defined. That way any per-sample factor shared by numerator and denominator cancels exactly. The overall sign is still the only thing fitted on the training fold.

The fitted members are trained on pooled sites, but AD prevalence differs between cohorts. So any protein shifted by site (pre-analytics or MS run) also carries label information, and the fitted logistic regressions learn site markers that cannot help with within-site ranking. I'm weighting training samples so that every (site, diagnosis) cell counts equally in the three fitted members. This makes site independent of label in the weighted fit, so the models can only learn contrasts that hold inside a cohort. Features stay unchanged, unlike the discarded site-centring in round 1, and site is used only for harmonization, never as a predictor.

The whole-proteome member's regularization strength (C=0.05, about 1,000 features, n≈110 per fold) was chosen arbitrarily. It is the noisiest fitted member. I now pick C by grouped inner CV on the training fold, scored by within-site AUROC to match the metric, so the shrinkage fits the actual signal-to-noise. Labels are used only inside the training fold. Not run yet; the harness score will show whether it helps.

The prior-biology panel model (b) is a free-sign L2 logistic regression on about 80 correlated proteins. At n≈110 per training fold, correlated proteins can end up with unstable, opposite-signed weights. I'm replacing it with a sign-constrained version: proteins whose direction in AD CSF is well established (glycolysis/14-3-3, glial and neuronal-injury proteins up; pentraxin/VGF/granin synaptic proteins down) must have coefficients in the literature direction. Proteins with no clear direction (the complement/amyloid/lipid module, BASP1, STMN1 and so on) stay unconstrained. Using known biology to cut estimator variance is what helped the weight-free ratio, but this version still fits magnitudes.

The sign-constrained panel model gained +0.0047 by removing unstable, opposite-signed weights on correlated proteins. This change applies the same idea to the whole-proteome member, which is still the noisiest fitted model (about 1,000 features, n≈110). Each protein's coefficient is now forced to share the sign of its own class difference on the training fold (a sign-consistent L2 logistic regression with the same C). That removes the suppressor patterns that do not transfer across folds or sites, without discarding any proteins. I haven't run this; the harness score will show whether it helps.

The module model (c) is still a free-sign logistic regression on five correlated module scores, and each score's PC1 orientation is arbitrary relative to AD. This change orients every module that has literature-directed members (glycolysis, glial, neuronal, synaptic) so its score points toward AD, then fits it with the same sign-constrained L2 logistic regression that helped the panel model in round 17. Those coefficients must be ≥ 0, while the complement/amyloid module stays unconstrained, which should remove unstable opposite-signed weights between correlated modules at n≈110. I haven't run it; the harness score will show whether it helps.

Right now each sample is centred on the median of whichever proteins it happened to quantify. In DIA, missingness depends on abundance, so a sample with poorer detection depth (fewer low-abundance proteins quantified) gets an inflated median and all its proteins shift down. That is a technical artifact that leaks into every member, including the ratio. I'm switching to a fixed reference set: each sample is centred on the median of the proteins quantified in nearly all samples (≥95%, with a fallback to lower thresholds), so every sample's normalization factor comes from the same proteins. This is label-free and done in `featurize`.
